lines.text: Two real failures happen here, genuinely different from each other: one of them is worth trying again, and the other one really isn't.
Each one is captured as its own real, named kind, matched directly against to decide whether to try again. Does matching it this way give the right call for both?
Yes, genuinely.
Matching against the real, specific kind it actually is gives the correct call every time.
Run it for real: matched against its own real kind, the one worth retrying gets retried, and the one that isn't gets correctly skipped.
The identical two failures are checked again, but this time only as the plain words each one happened to print, instead of their real, named kind.
Can those words alone still tell the two of them apart correctly?
No, genuinely.
Both of those failures happen to share the exact same words, so reading them can't tell them apart at all.
Run it for real: checked by those words alone, both failures now come back saying to try again, because the words genuinely can't tell the two of them apart.
Look specifically at the one failure that should never be retried.
Does the decision made from its real kind and the decision made from its plain words actually come out different?
Yes, genuinely, and that's the real problem.
One correctly says don't bother trying again; the other wrongly says go ahead and try.
Run it for real: on that exact same failure, the real-kind check correctly says don't retry, and the plain-words check wrongly says retry anyway, a genuine disagreement over the identical failure.
One real, independent page, and a second real, independent page right beside it, each describe the identical idea in their own words.

One says it offers a simple way to give code its own real, named kinds of failure. The other says it offers one, single kind that just carries whatever extra context a program wants to add as it goes.
So here's what this topic's own measurements are really standing in for: giving a real failure its own specific, named kind means whoever catches it can act correctly on exactly what happened.
Flattening that same failure down into plain words throws that away, and two genuinely different failures can end up looking identical once they're just words.
That isn't a small cosmetic difference. It's the real reason a retry call, or any decision like it, can come out wrong.
